items.title: Carbon monoxide's dipole points the wrong way
items.claim: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon (3.44 versus 2.55). You would expect carbon monoxide to have a dipole with the negative end on oxygen. In fact the negative end sits on carbon.
items.prompt: Why does CO's dipole point from O (positive) to C (negative)?

options.text: Electronegativity values are wrong for small molecules
Oxygen donates a lone pair into a bonding orbital concentrated on carbon — the dative pi back-bonding cancels and reverses the simple electronegativity dipole
Carbon monoxide has no dipole at all
The molecule rotates so fast the dipole averages to zero

items.reveal_title: Molecular orbital theory beats Pauling's electronegativity table
items.reveal:
Drawing CO with a triple bond shows it as :C≡O: with a lone pair on each atom. But molecular orbital calculations and experiment agree: the highest occupied molecular orbital is the sigma orbital pointing AWAY from oxygen on the carbon side, giving carbon partial negative character.

This is exactly why CO is such a good ligand for transition metals — it bonds to metals through the carbon, donating that lone pair while accepting back-donation into empty pi-star orbitals. The whole of transition-metal carbonyl chemistry depends on it.
items.why: Electronegativity gives a crude bond-polarity estimate. For molecules with multiple bonds and lone pairs, the orbital picture matters more.

items.title: A catalyst can be a product
items.claim: Autocatalytic reactions speed up as they proceed. The classic example: the oxidation of oxalic acid by permanganate. Manganese(II) ions, a product, catalyse the very reaction that makes them.
items.prompt: What does the rate-time curve look like for an autocatalytic reaction?

options.text: A constant rate from start to finish
S-shaped: slow start, accelerating middle, then slowing again as reactants run out
A straight line decreasing to zero
A spike at the start, then decay

items.reveal_title: Sigmoidal kinetics — a chemical population explosion
items.reveal:
At the start there is little catalyst, so the rate is slow. As Mn2+ builds up, rate accelerates. Eventually permanganate runs out and the rate falls. The curve is identical in shape to bacterial growth, viral epidemics or chain reactions — all are autocatalytic.

Life itself may be a form of autocatalysis: replication makes more replicators. Some prebiotic chemistry research focuses on finding the first autocatalytic networks that could bootstrap life on Earth.
items.why: Most introductory examples show monotonic rates. Autocatalysis breaks the simple 'rate falls as reactants decrease' story.

items.title: Doubling the nucleophile can do nothing
items.claim: Double the concentration of OH- in some nucleophilic substitutions and the rate doubles. In others, the rate doesn't change at all. Same reactants, same nucleophile, very different kinetics.
items.prompt: What controls whether the reaction is SN1 or SN2?

options.text: The structure of the substrate — tertiary halides go via a carbocation intermediate (SN1, rate-determining step doesn't involve nucleophile), primary halides go via concerted backside attack (SN2, rate depends on nucleophile)
The solvent — only polar solvents allow SN2
The atomic number of the halide

items.reveal_title: Mechanism is destiny — and rate law reveals mechanism
items.reveal:
Tertiary carbon centres are sterically blocked from backside SN2 attack but they form stable tertiary carbocations on dissociation. So they go SN1: slow ionisation followed by fast nucleophilic capture. The rate law is first order — only in the substrate.

Primary carbon centres can't make a stable carbocation but they're sterically open. They go SN2: concerted, one-step, with inversion of configuration. Rate law is second order: rate proportional to [substrate][nucleophile].

The same product (an alcohol from a halide) hides two completely different mechanisms with different stereochemistry: racemisation (SN1) versus inversion (SN2).
items.why: Rate laws are not just empirical — they are direct readouts of which mechanism is at work.
